The two-factor plugin, `@noctcore/auth/two-factor`, adds a TOTP second factor with recovery codes, trusted devices and step-up. Why each rule is there is in [Second factors](/auth/learn/second-factors/). Like the core, it has no HTTP endpoints: its flows live under `auth.twoFactor`, and your routes call them. This guide builds on [A Node server with Redis and Prisma](/auth/build/node-server/).

## The store and the cipher

The plugin needs a `TwoFactorStore` and a `SecretCipher`.

- **Store.** `PrismaTwoFactorStore` from `@noctcore/auth-prisma` (copy the four two-factor models from its `prisma/auth.prisma` and migrate) or `RedisTwoFactorStore` from `@noctcore/auth-redis`. The factor and the recovery codes are account data, so on Redis keep them only with persistence on. `MemoryTwoFactorStore` from `@noctcore/auth/testing` is for tests. Your own store must pass `twoFactorStoreConformance` (see [Writing a store adapter](/auth/build/store-adapter/)).
- **Cipher.** The plugin never sees a key. TOTP secrets are encrypted by the cipher you hand it, and only its output is stored. This one uses AES-256-GCM with the user id as associated data, and names its key in each ciphertext so you can rotate:

<Code code={cipherTs} lang="ts" title="src/two-factor/cipher.ts" />

Generate each key with `openssl rand -base64 32` and keep it with your other secrets, not in the database the ciphertexts live in. To rotate, add a key, make it current, and the old rows keep decrypting with the old one.

## Wiring the plugin

<Code code={authTs} lang="ts" title="src/auth.ts" />

| Option | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `store`, `cipher` | required | |
| `issuer` | required | The name the authenticator app shows. |
| `required` | never | `({ user }) => boolean`: users who must have a factor. Without one they get an enrollment challenge at login, never a session. |
| `enforcement` | off | `({ user }) => { required, graceEndsAt? }`: a requirement with a grace window, checked on every request; see [Enforcement with a grace period](#enforcement-with-a-grace-period). Pass it or `required`, not both. |
| `enforcementStanding` | `'live'` | `'at-issue'` (or `{ mode: 'at-issue', version }`): with `enforcement`, a session issued unrestricted skips the per-request reads; see [Standing decided at issue](#standing-decided-at-issue). |
| `enrollmentWindow` | `'10m'` | How long a pending secret from `enroll` accepts its confirmation code; positive, at most `'24h'`. See [Settings and step-up](#settings-and-step-up). |
| `stepUpWindow` | `'10m'` | How long a code proved in a session counts for sensitive actions. |
| `trustedDevices` | `{ ttl: '30d', maxPerUser: 5 }` | `false` turns "remember this device" off (and stops honouring devices trusted before). `ttl` must be at least a minute (the allowed clock skew) shorter than the session store's `epochTtlMs` (the Redis store's `epochTtl`). |
| `attempts` | 5 per `'15m'` | Code checks per user, from every IP together, before the factor locks. |
| `perIp` | 10 per `'1m'` | Code checks per IP. |
| `importedRecoveryCodes` | none | `{ hash }`: accept recovery codes carried over from your earlier scheme. See [Moving existing TOTP users over](#moving-existing-totp-users-over). |

Turning a factor on or off and spending a recovery code each send a mail event (`two-factor-enabled`, `two-factor-disabled`, `recovery-code-used`), so add them to your templates ([Mail](/auth/build/mail/)).

## Login

With the plugin on, `auth.login` answers `{ kind: 'challenge', challenge, methods }` for a user with a factor, after a correct password and without a session. The challenge lasts 5 minutes and takes 5 codes; it is bound to the browser's user agent. The browser sends it back with a code, a recovery code, or nothing but the trusted-device cookie:

<Code code={loginTs} lang="ts" title="src/routes/login.ts" />

Every refusal answers `invalid_second_factor` (or `rate_limited`); the reason, such as `wrong_code`, `code_replayed` or `factor_locked`, is only in the audit row. Show the same message for all of them.

Your `beforeSessionCreate` hooks run after a correct password, before any challenge is made (`via: 'password'`, `beforeChallenge: true`), and again for the session (`via: 'second-factor'`, or `'password'` when no challenge is due). An account they refuse gets `invalid_credentials`, counted as a wrong password in the lockout, and no challenge, so keep your sign-in refusals there and leave `code` at its default. With the plugin on, every password login runs them twice.

If your app re-issues the caller's session from a flow of its own (a password change, "sign out everywhere else"), issue it through a plugin's `context.issueSession(user, { via: 'my-flow', inherit: session, authenticatedAt: session.authenticatedAt, meta })`; pass `authenticatedAt` unless the flow just proved the password, or the old session comes back as freshly authenticated. For a user with a factor, it goes through only when `session` is live and was created after the enrollment window closed, or holds an open step-up (ask for one with `stepUp` otherwise). That is a best effort with known gaps (see Learn: Second factors), so turn the factor on with `revokeOtherSessions: true`. If the flow ends sessions first, call `context.confirmLiveSession(session)` before that and pass what it returns as `inherit`.

When `methods` is `['enroll']`, the user is one you require a factor of and has none yet. Pass the challenge to `auth.twoFactor.enroll({ challenge, meta })` to get a secret, show it, and send the first code to `verifyChallenge` as a TOTP proof: it turns the factor on and returns the session with the recovery codes.

## Sign-ins and checks your app runs itself

**A sign-in your app authenticated itself** (an identity provider's callback, a magic link of its own) gets the same challenge through `auth.twoFactor.challenge({ userId, rememberMe?, epoch?, meta })`. It answers `null` when no factor is due (the user has no confirmed factor and none is required, or there is no such user): issue your own session then. Otherwise it answers `{ challenge, methods }`, exactly as `auth.login` does, and `verifyChallenge` finishes it with a `second-factor` session that carries `rememberMe`; a trusted-device cookie passes it as after a password. Read `epoch` with `context.sessions.readEpoch(userId)` before your own credential check, so a revocation during it voids the session; without it the epoch is read when the challenge starts. Each call counts on the plugin's `perIp` limit, and the codes are counted at the verify on the factor's own budget. It does not run your `beforeSessionCreate` hooks before the challenge, since your own flow decided the user may sign in; they run for the session.

**A second factor without a session** (an app-owned reset, an invitation that overwrites an existing account's password) is checked with `auth.twoFactor.verifyProof({ userId, proof?, action, meta })`. Call it, with or without a proof, only for someone who already proved control of the account (a mailbox link, say, as `inspectPasswordReset` does), never on a form that names any account. Without `proof` it answers `ok({ proved: false })` when the user has no confirmed factor (or there is no such user) and `second_factor_required` when it has one: show the code field then. That answer reveals whether the account has a factor, and it writes no audit row. With `proof` it answers `ok({ proved: true })` for a right code and `invalid_second_factor` for anything else, a user with no factor or no user included, after the same store calls; show the code, not the `reason`. A right or wrong code for a user with a confirmed factor uses the challenge's budget, so wrong codes lock that factor (and climb the permanent lockout tier when you turned it on) just as at login: the reason to keep the call behind proof of control. A code for a user without one is counted on a key of its own and never locks the account or climbs the tier. It uses the challenge's replay guard and recovery-code spend (with its mail), writes `two_factor.verified` or `two_factor.failed` with your `action`, and never issues or touches a session. Every call, with or without a proof, counts on the plugin's `perIp` limit.

**An admin reset** of another user's factor is `auth.twoFactor.reset({ userId, actor?, meta })`, for a support agent who verified a locked-out user out of band. Call it only after your own checks: it trusts the caller. It deletes the factor (pending or confirmed), the recovery codes and the trusted devices, and answers `{ reset: true }`, or `{ reset: false }` with nothing done when there was no factor. A reset writes `two_factor.reset` (`userId` the user, `data.confirmed`, and `data.actor` your admin's id when you pass it), and a confirmed factor's owner gets `two-factor-disabled` with `reset: true`. The user's next login gets no challenge (or an enrollment challenge when you require a factor). Ending the user's sessions stays your call (`context.revokeAllSessions(userId, reason)`). A step-up proof a session already holds survives the reset until that session ends, so after a takeover revoke the sessions too. The mail is the same `two-factor-disabled` the owner gets for turning the factor off: make your template read `reset`, or it tells the user they turned it off themselves.

## Enforcement with a grace period

`required` is checked once, at login: a user without a factor never gets a session. When you turn the requirement on for users who already have accounts (a tenant that starts requiring a factor, say), give them a grace window with `enforcement` instead. Your policy answers per user, so the tenant, role or plan it hangs on stays in your app:

- **In the window**, sign-in works as usual and every validated session carries `twoFactor: { state: 'grace', graceEndsAt }` (milliseconds since the epoch). Show a reminder.
- **After the window**, the user still signs in, but the session is `twoFactor: { state: 'enrollment-only' }`: it reaches only the routes you mark for enrollment. Everything else answers `403` with `two_factor_enrollment_required`. Enrolling is the settings flow above (fresh password proof, `enroll`, `confirmEnrollment`); once the factor is confirmed the standing is gone on the next request.
- **Checked live.** The standing is computed on every request, never stored in the session, so a policy change or a closing window applies on the next request, without a new sign-in. The policy runs only for users without a confirmed factor (an enrolled user costs one store read), but it runs on each of their requests: cache your tenant rules (the example below expires and bounds its cache), and expect a change to apply once that cache does. `status` asks the policy once per call.
- **Or decided at issue.** With `enforcementStanding: 'at-issue'` the standing is also computed when a session is issued, and a session issued unrestricted is stamped and validates without any read. See [Standing decided at issue](#standing-decided-at-issue).
- **Fail closed.** A policy that throws, or answers nothing, reads as required with the window over (enrollment-only), and is logged by the error's name only. An unreadable `graceEndsAt` means no grace.
- **The sweep.** `auth.twoFactor.sweepUnenrolled({ userIds })` revokes every session of each listed user who is required, past the window and still without a confirmed factor, with reason `two-factor-required` (your `onSessionsRevoked` hook hears it). Each user is read again right before the revocation, so one who enrolled (or whose rule changed) during the sweep keeps their sessions. Users in the window, users with a factor and unknown ids are skipped; a user whose policy throws is skipped and counted in `failed`, since validation already confines that session. Pass any iterable or async iterable, so a large tenant can be paged from your database, and run it from your scheduler.

<Code code={enforcementTs} lang="ts" title="src/two-factor/enforcement.ts" />

With an adapter, mark what an enrollment-only session may reach: `@TwoFactorEnrollment()` on a NestJS route or controller ([NestJS](/auth/build/nestjs/#the-guard-order)), or `meta: { twoFactorEnrollment: true }` on a tRPC procedure ([tRPC](/auth/build/trpc/)). Mark the enrollment routes, `status`, re-authentication and sign out; the marker opens nothing else, so roles and fresh-auth still apply. Public routes and procedures run for anyone, so they ignore the standing: do not hand account data out of one. `status` reports the standing too, as `enforcement` (null when the factor is on or none is required).

### Standing decided at issue

The live check costs a factor read on every request of every user, and a user read and a policy call for each user without a factor. If most of your users are never required, `enforcementStanding: 'at-issue'` (with `enforcement`) keeps that cost off their requests.

**Which sessions skip the read.** A session issued while the user had a confirmed factor, or while your policy answered not required, carries a stamp (the `twoFactorStanding` session attribute) and validates without reading the factor, the user or the policy. Only a stamp of the current `version` at the session's own revocation epoch counts.

**Which sessions are read live.** Every other session, exactly as with `'live'`: one issued in the grace window or enrollment-only (so the window closing, enrolling or the policy lifting applies on the next request), one issued before you turned the option on or under another `version`, and one whose stamp your attribute schema dropped.

**Why a stamp is never stale.** Nothing about the user is read on a stamped session's requests, so every change that could restrict it ends it instead:

- **You require a factor of a user, or change their policy:** call `auth.twoFactor.refreshStanding({ userId })`. It ends the user's sessions (reason `two-factor-standing`; the epoch also voids their trusted devices), and their next sign-in is stamped from the new answer, so a user moved into a grace window signs in again to a grace session. Under `'live'` it does nothing (`revoked: false`), so you can call it either way.
- **A policy change for many users** (a tenant that starts requiring a factor): pass `enforcementStanding: { mode: 'at-issue', version }` with a new `version`. Sessions stamped under the old one are read live again, and the grace and enrollment-only standings apply on their next request.
- **An admin resets the factor** (`twoFactor.reset`): under `'at-issue'` it ends the user's sessions.
- **A sign-in that read the old answer just before a refresh** cannot keep a stamp: the stamp carries the epoch read before the answer, so a session minted after the refresh either loses the core's epoch fence or carries a stamp that does not match it (read live).
- **A re-issue** (a password change, say) is stamped again from the answer at that moment, never from the stamp it inherits.

A change you neither refresh nor version does not reach a stamped session until it ends; `sweepUnenrolled` still revokes the sessions of required users past their window, so keep running it. A policy whose answer changes with time by itself (required from a date) needs a refresh or a new version at that date. A deleted user's stamped session is not read either: end the sessions when you delete the user.

**Your attribute schema.** With `session.attributes`, let `twoFactorStanding` (a string) through. A schema that drops unknown keys only costs the reads; one that refuses them refuses every sign-in.

## Settings and step-up

Turning the factor on from the settings page needs a fresh password proof (`session.freshAuthAge`, 10 minutes by default; send the user through `auth.reauthenticate` if it is older). `enroll` returns the base32 `secret` and an `otpauth://` `uri` to show as a QR code. The secret becomes active only when a code from it comes back within `enrollmentWindow` (10 minutes by default, at most 24 hours; `expiresAt` follows it). A longer window helps users who set the authenticator up on another device or with help, but confirming still needs a fresh password proof, so past `session.freshAuthAge` send them through `auth.reauthenticate` first. An enrollment challenge (a required user at login) still ends with the challenge, 5 minutes, whatever the window. The window also dates when a factor counts as set up for your own re-issue of a session (a session created after it closed passes): shrinking it while enrollments are pending lets a session created between the new and the old end pass, so turn factors on with `revokeOtherSessions: true` if you shrink it.

<Code code={settingsTs} lang="ts" title="src/routes/settings.ts" />

`requireStepUp` is the guard for your own sensitive actions, such as deleting a project. Turning the factor off and new recovery codes already use it. A password change and an email change request accept the step-up held by the session, or a code with the request; you do not need to guard [email change](/auth/build/email-change/) yourself. Pass `revokeOtherSessions: true` to `confirmEnrollment` to sign out every other session when the factor goes on; set the cookie of the session it returns.

An email change revert never removes a factor: it cannot tell the owner's from one an intruder enrolled. An owner who cannot pass a factor the intruder enrolled needs support: support verifies the owner outside the account (the old mailbox alone proves nothing: the intruder may read it too), then resets the factor with `auth.twoFactor.reset({ userId, actor, meta })` (factor, recovery codes and trusted devices, audited and mailed) and has the owner reset the password. See [Email change](/auth/build/email-change/).

Other flows: `status(session)` (on, pending, required, recovery codes left), `regenerateRecoveryCodes`, `disable`, and `revokeTrustedDevices`. Password changes, resets and email change requests of a user with a factor take the code in `secondFactor` (six digits are read as a TOTP code, anything else as a recovery code); a password change or an email change request can skip it when the session holds a step-up. A reset page can learn before the user types anything whether the reset will ask for the code: `auth.inspectPasswordReset` answers `secondFactorRequired: true` for an account with a confirmed factor.

## Moving existing TOTP users over

If your users already have TOTP seeds, move each one into the store already confirmed, so their authenticator apps keep working. Their unused recovery codes can come along too (below):

<Code code={migrateTs} lang="ts" title="scripts/migrate-totp.ts" />

### Carrying recovery codes over

The plugin's own codes are stored as an HMAC keyed by your auth secret, so your old hashes cannot become plugin codes. They can still be accepted as they are, each once, if your old scheme hashed a code the same way every time (an unsalted or peppered SHA-256, an HMAC, a hash salted per user):

1. In the migration script, store each user's unused hashes with `importedRecoveryCodeHashes` (`migrateRecoveryCodes` above). It marks them as imported, so the plugin never confuses them with its own.
2. Tell the plugin how a typed code was hashed. `hash(code, { userId })` gets the input as typed (at most 64 characters) and returns the stored hash, or null when the input cannot be one of your codes. Normalise the way your old app did:

```ts
import { createHash } from 'node:crypto';

twoFactor({
  store,
  cipher,
  issuer: 'Acme',
  importedRecoveryCodes: {
    hash: (code) => {
      const compact = code.replace(/[\s-]/g, '').toUpperCase();

      return /^[0-9A-HJKMNP-TV-Z]{16}$/.test(compact)
        ? createHash('sha256').update(compact).digest('hex')
        : null;
    },
  },
});
```

Two things the hash has to live with:

- **It runs on every recovery-code proof, also one that is going to be refused.** A blocked or locked challenge, or a login for an unknown user, still hashes the input, so a refusal costs what a wrong code costs. On those paths `userId` is `NO_SUCH_USER_ID`, an id no store issues: do not assume the user exists, and do not look up anything that fails for an unknown id.
- **It should not throw.** A throw is logged (the error's name only) and read as no match, so the code is refused like a wrong one and the public answer is the same. The audit reason is not: when the input is not in the plugin's own code format either, the refusal is recorded as `malformed_recovery_code` rather than `wrong_recovery_code`.

An imported code is spent like any recovery code: by one atomic delete, counted in the factor budget, mailed to the owner (the audit row carries `imported: true`). When one passes the **login challenge** and the session is issued, the plugin replaces the user's whole set with ten new codes and `verifyChallenge` returns them in `recoveryCodes`: show them once, as after an enrollment. The mail and the audit row then count the new set (ten), not the old one. Of two logins at once with two different imported codes, only one replaces the set and shows it; the other gets its session with `recoveryCodes: null`, so no shown set is dead. If replacing the set fails (the store is down), the session stands, `recoveryCodes` is null and the failure is logged; the user can generate a new set from the settings page. If the login is refused after the code passed (a concurrent redemption of the challenge, a password change during it, one of your session hooks), the code is spent but the rest of the imported set stays and no new set is made. From then on the user is on the plugin's codes and the old hashes are gone from the store. An imported code spent on a step-up, a password change or a reset is spent without a new set (nothing there could show one); the user moves over at the next login that uses one, or by generating a new set from the settings page. Turning the option off later voids every imported code still in the store, so keep it until the users who have not moved yet are expected to re-enroll.

If your old codes were hashed with a per-code salt (bcrypt, Argon2), they cannot be looked up, so they cannot be carried over. Re-enroll those users instead: migrate the TOTP seed without recovery codes, and after their next sign-in send them to generate a new set from the settings page, where `status` shows `recoveryCodesRemaining: 0`. Until they do, the TOTP code is their only way through the challenge.

## Limits

TOTP does not stop a phishing page that relays the code in real time, and it does not protect a session cookie that was already stolen. See [Second factors](/auth/learn/second-factors/) for what the plugin does and does not cover.
